rationale: The source gives the same p>1/only-positive-divisors convention and composite complement. The item expands it with signed-divisor equivalence, explicit 0, 1, and negative boundaries, and the uniqueness motivation.

The sourced proof of Euclid's lemma explicitly uses the standard assertion p∤a => gcd(a,p)=1; the item packages that assertion with the complementary p|a case. Its dependency-indexed case proof is local.
The source states the same theorem for a,b in Z and prime p and supplies the same Bezout/coprimality proof.

The notes present the divisor definition and the product-divisibility definition as the two integer notions of prime in the unique-factorisation setting. The item makes their equivalence, the hypothesis p>1, and both directions explicit.
The source states that a prime dividing a finite product divides a factor. The item uses an indexed product of arbitrary integers and adds the empty-product boundary.
The source states the same existence theorem. The item supplies the least-divisor proof and spells out the divisor set and its least-element contract.
The source proves existence of a finite prime product for positive integers. The item recasts it as an indexed-list theorem, includes n=1 as the empty product, and adds the converse range clause.
The source gives existence and uniqueness up to rearrangement. The item expresses rearrangement as a permutation of finite von Neumann-indexed lists and treats the empty list explicitly.
The source states the same signed theorem for every nonzero integer, with a unit u=±1 and uniqueness of the unit and prime list up to rearrangement. The local proof is dependency-indexed.

The source gives Euclid's product-plus-one argument and infinitude conclusion. The item strengthens the presentation to every finite prime list and formalizes nonfiniteness by excluding an equinumeration with a natural; the proof adapts the classical construction.

The source defines the exponent of p in a nonzero integer as the greatest exponent for which the prime power divides it. The item constructs the maximum from boundedness and deliberately leaves v_p(0) undefined rather than adjoining infinity.

The source's integer valuation decomposition yields divisibility through the valuation, extraction of p^v with p-free cofactor, and the unit and prime values. The item separates these consequences and proves its local boundary conventions.

The sources state multiplicative additivity and the ultrametric lower bound. The item restricts the integer valuation to nonzero inputs and makes the nonzero-sum and natural-valued conventions explicit.

The source gives the unique prime-power form with distinct primes and natural exponents. The item indexes a prescribed covering list and identifies each exponent with the corresponding valuation, including zero off the list.
The source states a|b iff ν_p(a)≤ν_p(b) for every prime. The item specializes to positive integers so associates and undefined zero-valuations do not enter.
The sources give the minimum-exponent gcd and maximum-exponent lcm rules. The item adds positivity/definedness and proves that the recipes characterize the library's existing gcd and lcm.

The sources define v_p(a/b)=v_p(a)-v_p(b) on nonzero rationals and state well-definedness, additivity, and the ultrametric inequality. The item reconstructs these through the library's quotient representatives and embeddings.

The source proves that a rational kth root of a natural integer is an integer by the rational-root theorem. The item gives the signed-integer version in the library's rational embedding and proves it by valuations.

The exact bundle using 360 and 84—two factorisations, a four-prime valuation table, gcd/lcm, Euclidean descent, and product cross-check—is a bespoke worked construction rather than a recognizable literature proposition. Every displayed product, valuation, division, gcd, lcm, and cross-check was directly recomputed.
The source states and proves exactly that 2 is prime and every even integer greater than 2 is composite.

The sources establish irrationality of sqrt(3), the general non-square square-root criterion covering sqrt(6), and irrationality of the cube root of 2. The item conjoins the three claims in quotient-field notation and discharges them through its earlier rational-root corollary.
The source constructs arbitrarily long consecutive composite runs as N!+2 through N!+N. The item uses the semantically identical finite product 2·3···(n+1), shifts the indexing, and includes n=0.

The source defines Hilbert monoids H_m={x≥1:x≡1 mod m} and records failure of unique factorisation in arithmetic congruence monoids. The item specializes to H_3 and supplies the elementary irreducible witness 100=4·25=10·10.
The source gives the same failure: if 1 is prime, 6 has the factorizations 2·3, 1·2·3, 1·1·2·3, and so on. The item formalizes this as unequal list lengths under the modified definition.
The source states the same false conjecture and exact counterexample 1+2·3·5·7·11·13=30031=59·509. The item expands the arithmetic and composite check in library notation.
The source refutes the reindexed form n^2−n+41 at n=41 by 41^2=1681. Replacing its n by n+1 gives the item's n^2+n+41 counterexample at n=40; the proof expands that substitution.

The source states Fermat's conjecture, gives F_5=2^32+1, and proves 641 divides it from 641=2^4+5^4=5·2^7+1. The item reparameterizes the Fermat numbers by the power-of-two exponent and rewrites the sourced computation without congruence notation.
